hypotheses.text: Ectodermal manifestations—specifically sparse hair, coarse hair, or abnormal tooth/nail development—are mandatory discriminating criteria to clinically distinguish GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome from infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (PLA2G6/PLAN) and pontocerebellar hypoplasias, because pure neuroimaging findings (cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum) and motor trajectories (hypotonia progressing to spasticity with optic atrophy) overlap completely between the two conditions.
hypotheses.rationale: The previous hypothesis posited that neuroimaging (cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum) and neuromuscular features (hypotonia evolving to spasticity with optic atrophy) alone discriminate GTPBP2 from mimics such as PLA2G6. However, PLA2G6/PLAN produces an identical clinical and neuroimaging triad. In contrast, ectodermal signs like sparse hair occur in over 90% of GTPBP2 cases and are absent in classic PLA2G6-associated infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.

evidence.text: A comprehensive literature review of 28 individuals with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome found that sparse hair was present in 26 of 28 patients (92.9%), alongside motor development delay in 26 of 28 patients.

evidence.text: Delineation of GTPBP2-associated syndrome identifies it as a distinct neuro-ectodermal condition where key distinguishing features include ectodermal dysplasia and retinal dysfunction in addition to tone abnormalities and brain iron accumulation.

source.quote: Key features of this clinically recognizable condition include prenatal onset microcephaly, tone abnormalities, and movement disorders, epilepsy, dysmorphic features, retinal dysfunction, ectodermal dysplasia, and brain iron accumulation.

evidence.text: GTPBP2 is recognized as an etiology of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), a category that also contains PLA2G6 (PLAN), indicating significant overlap in central nervous system neurodegenerative pathology.

hypotheses.text: Basal ganglia iron accumulation on brain MRI is absent in early infancy and childhood in GTPBP2-related disorder, precluding its utility as an early discriminator from non-iron-accumulating pontocerebellar hypoplasias or spastic paraplegias.
hypotheses.rationale: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation is cited as a feature of GTPBP2, but literature reports suggest that basal ganglia iron deposition is age-dependent and typically undetectable during the initial infantile or early childhood diagnostic presentation.

evidence.text: Review of GTPBP2 patients indicates phenotypic evolution where brain iron accumulation appears only after childhood, and ectodermal findings as well as neuropathy become more prominent in older patients.

source.title: Clinical delineation of GTPBP2‐associated neuro‐ectodermal syndrome: Report of two new families and review of the literature
source.quote: Our findings suggest that some aspects of the clinical presentation appear to be age-related; brain iron accumulation may appear only after childhood, and the ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are most prominent in older individuals.

evidence.text: Earlier cohort descriptions of three unrelated families with biallelic GTPBP2 inactivating variants noted absence of brain iron accumulation in those pediatric patients, highlighting that structural abnormalities like corpus callosum dysgenesis and cerebellar hypoplasia appear earlier than iron deposition.

source.title: Biallelic inactivating variants in the GTPBP2 gene cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with severe intellectual disability
source.quote: Notable differences include structural brain abnormalities (e.g., agenesis of the corpus callosum, exclusive to our patients), and evidence for brain iron accumulation (exclusive to the previously described family).

hypotheses.text: Corpus callosum agenesis or hypogenesis is present in only a subset of GTPBP2 patients and therefore its absence on neuroimaging does not rule out Jaberi-Elahi syndrome when progressive cerebellar atrophy, microcephaly, and sparse hair are present.
hypotheses.rationale: While thinning or agenesis of the corpus callosum is frequently cited as part of the core discriminating tetrad, reports across multiple cohorts show variable penetrance of callosal dysgenesis, meaning it cannot serve as an obligate diagnostic criterion.

evidence.text: Structural brain abnormalities such as agenesis or hypogenesis of the corpus callosum were prominent in newly identified families but absent in the original family reported by Jaberi et al., demonstrating inter-familial variability in callosal involvement.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence and specificity of ectodermal dysplasia features (hypotrichosis, sparse hair, dental abnormalities) in GTPBP2 patients versus PLA2G6, CASK, and TSEN cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Resolving whether sparse hair and ectodermal findings achieve >90% sensitivity in GTPBP2 while remaining near 0% in PLA2G6 and PCH will provide a definitive clinical algorithmic rule for differential diagnosis prior to molecular sequencing.

new_directions.question_text: At what median age does brain iron accumulation become visible on T2*/SWI MRI sequences in GTPBP2-related disorder?
new_directions.rationale: Determining the exact age of onset of radiological iron accumulation in the basal ganglia will prevent premature exclusion of GTPBP2 in infants who show cerebellar atrophy and hypotonia without iron deposition.
